mainTopic: Which מצוות bind בני נח (מילה, פריה ורביה, גיד הנשה), meat for אדם and בני נח, and רבי שמעון on כישוף
overview: The amud opens by testing the rule that a מצוה given to בני נח and repeated at סיני applies to everyone. מילה and פריה ורביה seem to break the rule. The גמרא answers that their 'repeats' at סיני only came to teach new points: מילה on שבת, and that a ban made by vote needs a new vote to lift it. It then explains that only a full restatement of the prohibition counts, and that גיד הנשה is the one מצוה never repeated at all. A second answer says מילה was given only to אברהם's offspring through יעקב, with קטורה's descendants added by a separate פסוק. Next, רב teaches that אדם הראשון could not eat meat, while בני נח were allowed meat but not אבר מן החי. The גמרא defends רב by reading 'ורדו' as using animals for work, including fish, birds and the snake, and explains that the angels gave אדם meat from heaven. The amud ends as רבי שמעון adds כישוף to the מצוות בני נח, and the פסוק for his view comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Challenge from circumcision
steps.stepSummary: מילה was told to אברהם, who still counted as one of בני נח, and repeated at סיני. Yet it applies only to ישראל, which seems to break the rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about מילה? It was said to בני נח: 'And you shall keep My covenant.' It was repeated at סיני: 'And on the eighth day he shall be circumcised.' Yet it was said only for ישראל and not for בני נח!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the rule from earlier on the daf with a counter-example. מילה fits the pattern 'said to בני נח and repeated at סיני', but it does not apply to non-Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule says a מצוה that was repeated at סיני applies to everyone. מילה was commanded to אברהם before סיני, while he still had the status of בני נח, and it shows up again in ויקרא. Even so, non-Jews are not commanded in מילה, so the rule seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: But look at / but isn't there (opens a counter-example)
Descendants of Noah, meaning all non-Jews
And it was repeated at Mount סיני

steps.confusionAlert: אברהם is counted here as one of בני נח, because the Torah had not yet been given. That is why a command to him counts as 'said to בני נח'.

phrases.english: But there is circumcision,
which was said to the descendants of Noah,
phrases.notes: He means אברהם, who before סיני still counted as one of בני נח.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'And you shall keep My covenant,'
phrases.notes: בראשית 17:9

phrases.english: and it was repeated at Sinai:
'And on the eighth day he shall be circumcised' —
phrases.notes: ויקרא 12:3

phrases.english: yet it was said to Israel and not to the descendants of Noah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the general rule about repeated מצוות, which was stated earlier on the daf.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a מצוה said to בני נח and repeated at סיני applies to both groups.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counter-example: מילה fits the rule's conditions but applies only to ישראל.

steps.title: The Sinai verse came to permit מילה on שבת
steps.stepSummary: The verse at סיני was not a repeat of the מצוה. It came to teach that מילה on the eighth day is done even on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse came to permit שבת: 'on the day' means even on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the סיני verse about מילה does not count as a 'repeat'. It was needed to teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'on the eighth day' teach that מילה must happen on that exact day, even if it falls on שבת. Since the verse came for this new law, it is not counted as restating the מצוה. So the rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: That is what it comes for
On the day (the exact day, no matter what)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source that מילה on the eighth day pushes aside the איסורים of שבת.

phrases.english: That verse — to permit Shabbat
is what it comes for,
'On the day' — and even on Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from מילה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the second verse as teaching a new law, so it is not a true repetition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ויקרא verse simply restates the מצוה of מילה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse teaches that מילה pushes aside שבת, so מילה was never truly 'repeated' at סיני.

steps.title: Challenge from having children
steps.stepSummary: פריה ורביה was said to בני נח and seems to be repeated at סיני. Yet it applies only to ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about פריה ורביה? It was said to בני נח: 'And you, be fruitful and multiply.' It was repeated at סיני: 'Go say to them, return to your tents.' Yet it was said only for ישראל and not for בני נח!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second counter-example to the same rule, this time the מצוה of having children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נח's family was told to have children. At סיני, after the men were told to stay away from their wives to prepare for מתן תורה, they were told to 'return to your tents', meaning back to their wives. That looks like a repeat of the מצוה, yet non-Jews are not obligated in it.

keyTerms.meaning: Return to your tents (go back to your wives)

phrases.english: But there is being fruitful and multiplying,
which was said to the descendants of Noah,
as it is written: 'And you, be fruitful and multiply,'
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:7

phrases.english: and it was repeated at Sinai:
'Go say to them: Return to your tents' —
phrases.notes: דברים 5:27. The men had stayed away from their wives before מתן תורה, and now they were told to go back to them.

phrases.english: yet it was said to Israel and not to the descendants of Noah!

steps.triggerLanguage: וַהֲרֵי פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה שֶׁנֶּאֶמְרָה לִבְנֵי נֹחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the same rule, built the same way as step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a מצוה said to בני נח and repeated at סיני applies to both groups.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Counter-example: פריה ורביה fits the conditions but applies only to ישראל.

steps.title: The Sinai verse teaches that a vote needs a vote to undo it
steps.stepSummary: 'Return to your tents' was not a repeat of פריה ורביה. It teaches that something forbidden by an official vote needs another vote to permit it.
steps.simpleTranslation: That verse came to teach that anything forbidden by a vote needs another vote to permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'return to your tents' was needed for a different lesson, so it does not count as a repeat of the מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once מתן תורה was over, the reason for staying away from their wives was gone. Even so, הקב״ה had to say so openly. This teaches that a ban made by an official ruling does not end by itself; it needs a new ruling to cancel it. So פריה ורביה was never truly repeated, and the rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A count / official vote of the חכמים

steps.whatToRemember: Both challenges get the same kind of answer. The סיני verse was needed to teach a new הלכה (מילה on שבת, or 'a vote needs a vote'), so it does not count as a 'repeat'. The rule about בני נח survives.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the principle דבר שבמנין צריך מנין אחר להתירו: a rabbinic ban stays in force until it is officially cancelled, even if its reason seems gone.

phrases.english: That verse — for any matter that was decided by a vote
phrases.notes: The separation before מתן תורה was an official command, so the verse treats it like a ban decided by a vote.

phrases.english: requires another vote to permit it
is what it comes for.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא לְכׇל דָּבָר שֶׁבְּמִנְיָן צָרִיךְ מִנְיָן אַחֵר לְהַתִּירוֹ הוּא דַּאֲתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from פריה ורביה, in the same style as step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the second verse as teaching a new law, so it is not a true repetition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Return to your tents' restates the מצוה of פריה ורביה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse teaches that a ban made by vote needs a new vote to lift it, so פריה ורביה was not repeated at סיני.

steps.title: If so, every repeated מצוה could be explained away
steps.stepSummary: If repeats can be explained as teaching a new detail, then every one of the שבע מצוות בני נח could be explained the same way. That would make all of them apply only to ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, we could also say about each and every one that it was repeated only because of some other point.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answers from steps 2 and 4. If those answers work, they seem to work for every מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 2 and 4 said the repeat at סיני was only there to teach a new detail. But almost every מצוה repeated at סיני could be said to teach some detail. Then nothing would count as truly repeated, and none of the מצוות בני נח would still apply to non-Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if your answer is right

phrases.english: If so,
about each and every one too,
phrases.notes: He means each of the שבע מצוות בני נח.

phrases.english: let us say it was repeated because of some other point?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, כֹּל חֲדָא וַחֲדָא נָמֵי נֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the type of answer used in steps 2 and 4
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a repeat at סיני was only there to teach a new detail
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That answer proves too much. It would cancel every repeat, so no מצוה would apply to both בני נח and ישראל.

steps.title: Repeating the full prohibition is what counts
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah only wanted to teach a detail, it did not need to restate the whole prohibition. When the whole prohibition is restated, that shows it applies to both groups.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he means: why would the Torah need to go back and repeat the prohibition itself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the rule of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא really means by 'repeated.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Teaching a new detail does not require restating the full prohibition. So when the Torah does restate the whole prohibition, that extra wording teaches that the מצוה applies to both בני נח and ישראל. The repeats of מילה and פריה ורביה were not full restatements. They were only there for a detail.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he means: an explanation of someone's words
A prohibition, a warning not to do something

phrases.english: This is what he is saying:
phrases.notes: This is explaining the rule of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא that the whole discussion is built on.

phrases.english: to go back and repeat the prohibition itself,
why do I need that?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any mention at סיני might count as a repeat, and any repeat could be explained away as a detail
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a full restatement of the prohibition counts. That extra wording shows the מצוה applies to both groups.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the test for the whole rule: did the Torah restate the actual prohibition, or did it only mention the מצוה to teach a detail?

steps.title: Why is גיד הנשה called the only example?
steps.stepSummary: The earlier statement said גיד הנשה is the only מצוה told to בני נח that applies just to ישראל. But מילה and פריה ורביה were also not truly repeated, so they should count too.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And we have only גיד הנשה, according to רבי יהודה.' But these were not repeated either!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the line saying גיד הנשה is the only example. Then it challenges that line, based on the answers about מילה and פריה ורביה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that גיד הנשה was already forbidden before סיני, so it fits the category of 'told before סיני and applies only to ישראל.' But steps 2 and 4 showed that מילה and פריה ורביה were not truly repeated either. So why does the statement say גיד הנשה is the only example?

keyTerms.meaning: The sciatic nerve, which is forbidden to eat
According to the view of רבי יהודה

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לָנוּ אֶלָּא גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה בִּלְבַד,
phrases.english: 'And we have only גיד הנשה alone,'
phrases.notes: This quotes the end of the earlier statement: גיד הנשה is the one מצוה told before סיני that applies only to ישראל.

phrases.english: 'and that is according to רבי יהודה.'
These, too, were not repeated!
phrases.notes: 'These' means מילה and פריה ורביה from steps 1 through 4.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין לָנוּ אֶלָּא גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה בִּלְבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the answers already given to challenge the claim that there is only one example
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that גיד הנשה is the only example
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If מילה and פריה ורביה were not truly repeated, they also apply only to ישראל. So גיד הנשה cannot be the only one.

steps.title: Repeated for a detail versus never repeated at all
steps.stepSummary: מילה and פריה ורביה were at least repeated for some other point. גיד הנשה was never repeated at all, so it is the only clean example of the category.
steps.simpleTranslation: These were repeated for some other point. This one was not repeated at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 7 by separating two kinds of 'not repeated.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: מילה and פריה ורביה do appear again at סיני, even though only to teach a detail. So they are not listed as 'not repeated.' גיד הנשה never appears again at all, so it alone fits the category of 'told to בני נח and not repeated at סיני.'

keyTerms.meaning: Merely, just: for some general point

steps.whatToRemember: גיד הנשה (according to רבי יהודה) is the only מצוה told before סיני and never repeated at all. מילה and פריה ורביה were repeated, but only to teach a detail. Either way, all three apply only to ישראל.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this answer makes מילה and פריה ורביה apply to non-Jews. They still apply only to ישראל. They are just not the example the statement had in mind for 'never repeated.'

phrases.english: These were repeated just for the sake of some other point,
but this one was not repeated at all.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is גיד הנשה, which appears only in בראשית.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מילה and פריה ורביה should also be listed with גיד הנשה
steps.terutzMaskana: Only גיד הנשה was never repeated at all. The others were repeated for some other point, so they are not in that list.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The statement 'we have only גיד הנשה' refers to a מצוה with no repeat at all at סיני.

steps.title: Circumcision was only given to אברהם and his offspring
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: מילה never applied to all בני נח. From the start it was commanded only to אברהם and his offspring.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, give a different answer: from the very start, the Torah commanded מילה only to אברהם, as it says, "And you shall keep My covenant, you and your offspring after you, for their generations." "You and your offspring" are included. Anyone else is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to explain why מילה is not a מצוה for all בני נח. It says the command was never given to them in the first place, only to אברהם and his family.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 said the סיני verse about מילה came to teach a new point, so it is not a true repeat. This answer takes a different path. מילה was never a בני נח מצוה at all, because the פסוק limits it to "you and your offspring." That wording excludes every other person.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say (introduces another answer)
The Merciful One (God, through the Torah)
My covenant (here, the covenant of מילה)

phrases.english: If you want, say:
Circumcision, from the very start, it was to Avraham
that the Merciful One commanded it,
"And you shall keep My covenant,
phrases.notes: בראשית 17:9

phrases.english: you and your offspring after you, for their generations."
"You and your offspring": yes,
another person: no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the step 1 challenge from מילה, alongside the step 2 answer: מילה was never commanded to בני נח at all. This also explains why מילה is not grouped with גיד הנשה (steps 7–8).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative source reading: the original command was limited to אברהם's family
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מילה seemed to be a מצוה given to בני נח and then repeated at סיני, so by the rule it should apply to בני נח too.
steps.terutzMaskana: מילה was never commanded to בני נח at all. It was given only to אברהם and his offspring, so it doesn't belong in that category.

steps.title: Then ישמעאל's descendants should be obligated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: ישמעאל is also אברהם's son, so his descendants should have to do מילה too.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, the descendants of ישמעאל should be obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the new answer. If "your offspring" are obligated, ישמעאל's children are אברהם's offspring too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 9 makes the obligation depend on being אברהם's offspring. ישמעאל is a real son of אברהם, so the rule seems to cover his line as well. The גמרא assumes this is not the case, so the answer needs fixing.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (now you must accept this result)

phrases.english: But if so,
the descendants of Yishmael should be obligated!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the step 9 answer by pointing to another son of אברהם.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that "you and your offspring" means all of אברהם's descendants
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ישמעאל is אברהם's offspring, so by step 9's logic his descendants must be obligated in מילה.

steps.title: Only יצחק's line counts as אברהם's offspring
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק teaches that only through יצחק are descendants called אברהם's offspring, so ישמעאל's line is not included.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: "For through יצחק shall offspring be called yours."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. It shows that ישמעאל's children are not counted as "your offspring" for this purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "offspring" in the מילה command is defined by this פסוק. Only יצחק's line is called אברהם's offspring. That leaves ישמעאל's descendants outside the obligation.

phrases.english: "For through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours."
phrases.notes: בראשית 21:12

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the step 10 challenge about ישמעאל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining a word through another פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All of אברהם's children, including ישמעאל, count as his offspring.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only יצחק's line is called אברהם's offspring, so ישמעאל's descendants are excluded.

steps.title: Then עשו's descendants should be obligated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: עשו is יצחק's son, so his descendants should have to do מילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then the descendants of עשו should be obligated!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes further. If יצחק's line counts, then עשו, who is יצחק's son, should be included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 narrowed "offspring" to יצחק's line. עשו belongs to that line, so the narrowed rule still seems to include him. The גמרא assumes his descendants are not obligated, so another limit is needed.

phrases.english: The descendants of Esav should be obligated!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the step 11 answer by pointing to a son of יצחק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that יצחק's line counts as אברהם's offspring
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: עשו is part of יצחק's line, so his descendants should be obligated in מילה.

steps.title: Only part of יצחק's line is included
steps.stepSummary: The word "ביצחק" means "some of יצחק," not all of יצחק's descendants. This excludes עשו.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Through יצחק" means part of יצחק, and not all of יצחק.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the same פסוק more closely. The small letter ב shows that only part of יצחק's family is meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prefix ב in בְּיִצְחָק is read as "of" or "from within" יצחק. That limits the offspring to only some of his descendants. עשו's line is left out, leaving only יעקב's line.

keyTerms.meaning: The letter ב, read here as "part of"

phrases.english: "Through Yitzchak": and not all of Yitzchak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the step 12 challenge about עשו.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Close reading of a single letter in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All of יצחק's descendants, including עשו, count as אברהם's offspring.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only part of יצחק's line counts, so עשו's descendants are excluded.

steps.title: רב אושעיא: קטורה's descendants are included, though not from יצחק
steps.stepSummary: רב אושעיא challenges: by this logic, the descendants of קטורה would be exempt. Yet a known teaching includes them in מילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אושעיא challenged this: But if so, the descendants of קטורה should not be obligated! Didn't רבי יוסי בר אבין say (and some say it was רבי יוסי בר חנינא) that "He has broken My covenant" comes to include the descendants of קטורה?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אושעיא attacks the whole "offspring through יצחק" approach. קטורה's children are not from יצחק, yet a teaching obligates them in מילה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 11 and 13 limited מילה to part of יצחק's line. קטורה's children come from אברהם but not through יצחק, so they should be exempt. But a teaching from the words "He has broken My covenant" explicitly includes them, which contradicts the limit.

keyTerms.meaning: The descendants of קטורה, אברהם's later wife

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read "הָאָמַר" as a new answer. It means "but didn't he say?" רב אושעיא is quoting this teaching to make his challenge stronger.
steps.whyThisMatters: This challenge shows that "only יצחק's line" can't be the full story, because another group from אברהם is also obligated.

phrases.english: Rav Oshaya challenged this:

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה לָא לִחַיְּיבוּ?
phrases.english: But if so, the descendants of Keturah should not be obligated?
But didn't Rabbi Yosei bar Avin say,
and some say it was Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina:
"He has broken My covenant":
phrases.notes: בראשית 17:14

phrases.english: this comes to include the descendants of Keturah.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אוֹשַׁעְיָא: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, בְּנֵי קְטוּרָה לָא לִחַיְּיבוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the whole step 9–13 approach of limiting מילה to part of יצחק's line.
steps.kashyaTarget: The limit of מילה to part of יצחק's descendants
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קטורה's descendants are not from יצחק, so the limit exempts them. Yet a teaching from "את בריתי הפר" includes them in מילה, which contradicts the limit.

steps.title: The first man was not allowed to eat meat
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: אדם הראשון was not allowed to eat meat. He learns this from a פסוק that gives plants as food to both people and animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: אדם הראשון was not permitted to eat meat, as it says "For you it shall be for food, and for every animal of the earth." This means the animals of the earth are not food for you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a statement from רב: אדם הראשון was not allowed to eat meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק lists people and animals side by side as the ones who eat plants. Because animals are listed as fellow eaters, they are not themselves food for people.
steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying אדם was forbidden to use animals. He is only saying אדם was not allowed to eat them.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
The first man was not permitted
meat for eating,
as it is written: "For you it shall be for food,
phrases.notes: בראשית 1:29–30

phrases.english: and for every animal of the earth",
but the animals of the earth are not for you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the מילה discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אדם הראשון was forbidden to eat meat.

steps.title: בני נח were allowed to eat meat
steps.stepSummary: When בני נח came, eating meat was permitted to them, based on the פסוק "as the green herb I have given you all."
steps.simpleTranslation: When the children of Noah came, He permitted meat to them, as it says: "As the green herb, I have given you everything."
steps.whatsHappening: The statement goes on: after the מבול, בני נח were allowed to eat meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק compares meat to plants. Plants were already permitted to אדם, and now meat is permitted to בני נח in the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Noah's descendants, meaning all of mankind

phrases.english: And when the children of Noah came, He permitted it to them,
as it is stated: "As the green herb
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:3

phrases.english: I have given you everything."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב's statement and shows how the איסור changed with Noah.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat was permitted to בני נח.

steps.title: Eating a limb from a living animal is still forbidden
steps.stepSummary: One might think that once meat is fully permitted, even אבר מן החי is allowed. The פסוק "אך בשר בנפשו דמו לא תאכלו" teaches that it is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think the איסור of a limb from a living animal does not apply to them. So the פסוק says: "Only flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat."
steps.whatsHappening: The text limits the new permission. בני נח may eat meat, but not a limb cut from an animal that is still alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "בשר בנפשו" means meat while the animal's life is still in it. So the general permission to eat meat has an exception for אבר מן החי.

keyTerms.meaning: A limb taken from a living animal
With its life still in it

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source that אבר מן החי is one of the שבע מצוות בני נח.

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל לֹא יְהֵא אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי
phrases.english: One might think that the limb from a living animal
would not apply to him?
phrases.notes: "Him" means a בן נח.

phrases.english: Therefore the verse states: "Only flesh with its life,
phrases.notes: בראשית 9:4

phrases.english: its blood, you shall not eat."

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל לֹא יְהֵא אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי נוֹהֵג בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the permission given in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אבר מן החי remains forbidden to בני נח.

steps.title: Creeping animals are not included in this prohibition
steps.stepSummary: One might think the איסור of אבר מן החי also applies to שרצים. The word "אך" (only) excludes them.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think it applies even to creeping animals. So the פסוק says "only."
steps.whatsHappening: The text narrows the איסור again. For בני נח, אבר מן החי does not include שרצים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "אך" is a word that limits. Here it shows that the איסור does not cover every creature, and שרצים are left out.

keyTerms.meaning: Only; a word that limits or excludes

phrases.english: One might think it applies even to creeping animals?
Therefore the verse states: "Only."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the איסור from step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For בני נח, אבר מן החי does not apply to שרצים.

steps.title: How do we know creeping animals are the ones left out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the reasoning is. "אך" only tells us something is excluded, so why should it be שרצים?
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the derivation?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind excluding שרצים in particular. It is setting up רב הונא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "אך" shows that some creature is excluded, but it does not say which one. The גמרא wants a hint in the פסוק that points to שרצים.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the reasoning or derivation?

phrases.english: And what is the derivation?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is it שרצים that are excluded from אבר מן החי?

steps.title: Only creatures whose blood is separate from their flesh
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא: the word "דמו" teaches that the איסור is about creatures whose blood counts as separate from their flesh. שרצים are not like that, so they are excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: "Its blood" means a creature whose blood is separate from its flesh. This excludes creeping animals, whose blood is not separate from their flesh.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers the question: the word "דמו" in the פסוק points to which creatures are included, and שרצים are not among them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק talks about "its blood," so it covers creatures whose blood is something separate from the meat. For שרצים, the blood counts as part of the flesh, so they fall outside the איסור.
steps.whatToRemember: For בני נח, אבר מן החי applies to creatures whose blood is separate from their flesh. שרצים are excluded because of the word "דמו".

phrases.english: Rav Huna said: "Its blood"
means one whose blood is separate from its flesh,
excluding creeping animals,
whose blood is not separate from their flesh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word "דמו" limits the איסור to creatures whose blood is separate from their flesh, which leaves out שרצים.

steps.title: Challenge: the man was told to rule over the fish
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב from "ורדו בדגת הים". Doesn't ruling over the fish mean being allowed to eat them?
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: "And have dominion over the fish of the sea." Isn't that talking about eating?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רב's statement in step 15 and challenges it with a פסוק said to אדם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אדם was told to rule over the animals, it seems he could eat them. That would go against רב's claim that meat was forbidden to him.

phrases.english: They raised an objection: "And have dominion over the fish of the sea";
phrases.notes: בראשית 1:28

phrases.english: is it not for eating?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to challenge רב's opening statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that אדם הראשון was forbidden to eat meat.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being given control over the animals suggests permission to eat them.

steps.title: Answer: ruling over animals means using them for work
steps.stepSummary: No. "ורדו" means using animals for work, not eating them.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means for labor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: the power אדם was given over animals was to use them for work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Ruling over" can mean using animals to help you, without eating them. So the פסוק does not go against רב.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, אדם could use animals for work but could not eat them. Meat was only permitted from בני נח onward.

phrases.english: No, for labor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzMaskana: "ורדו" means using animals for work, so רב's statement stands.

steps.title: Can fish really do work?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the last answer: fish cannot be used for work, so 'ורדו בדגת הים' must mean eating them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And are fish able to do work?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 22. If 'ורדו' means using animals for work, how can it apply to fish?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 said 'ורדו' is about work, not eating. But the פסוק includes fish, and fish do not seem able to work at all. So it seems 'ורדו' must mean eating after all, at least for fish.

phrases.english: And are fish capable of work?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 22 that 'ורדו' means work.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'ורדו' refers to using animals for work.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Fish seem unable to work, so ruling over fish must mean eating them.

steps.title: Yes, fish can work, as shown by רחבה's question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that fish can work in some way, as shown by רחבה, who asked about driving a goat and a fish together.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, like רחבה. For רחבה asked: if someone drove a wagon with a goat and a שיבוטא fish, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that fish can in fact be used for work. It proves this from a question asked by רחבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רחבה asked about someone who drove a goat and a שיבוטא fish together. His question is about the איסור of working with two different kinds of animals together. The fact that he could even ask it shows that a fish can, at least in theory, pull a load.

keyTerms.meaning: he drove (led animals pulling a load)

steps.confusionAlert: רחבה is not saying people normally work with fish. His question only shows that it is possible in some unusual way, and that is enough to answer the challenge.

phrases.english: Yes, in accordance with Rachava.
For Rachava asked:
If one drove with a goat and a shibbuta fish, what is the law?
phrases.notes: He is asking if this counts as working with two different kinds of animals together, which the Torah forbids.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual proof that the challenge's assumption is wrong (fish can work).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Fish cannot work, so 'ורדו' must mean eating.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fish can work, as רחבה's question shows, so 'ורדו' can still mean work.

steps.title: A new challenge from 'the birds of the sky'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another proof from the same פסוק: ruling over the birds must mean eating them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'And over the birds of the sky.' Isn't this about eating?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries another proof against רב, from the next words in the same פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק also says to rule over the birds. The גמרא suggests this must mean eating the birds. If so, אדם הראשון was allowed to eat meat.

phrases.english: Come and hear: "And over the birds of the sky."
phrases.notes: בראשית 1:28

phrases.english: Is it not referring to eating?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the fish challenge was answered, a parallel challenge comes from birds.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view that אדם הראשון was not allowed to eat meat.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ruling over birds must mean eating them, so meat was allowed.

steps.title: No, it means work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the same answer as before: ruling over birds means using them for work.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means for work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the bird challenge the same way it answered about fish: 'ורדו' means work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer applies the rule from Step 22 to birds as well. It also sets up the next question, since it is not obvious that birds can work.

phrases.english: No, it refers to work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 25.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ruling over birds means eating them.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ruling over birds means using them for work.

steps.title: Can birds really do work?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer: can birds actually be used for work?
steps.simpleTranslation: And are birds able to do work?
steps.whatsHappening: Just like with fish, the גמרא questions whether birds can work. If they cannot, the answer in Step 26 falls apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Birds do not seem to be work animals. If they cannot work, ruling over them would have to mean eating them.

phrases.english: And are birds capable of work?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that ruling over birds means using them for work.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Birds seem unable to work, so 'ורדו' must mean eating them.

steps.title: Yes, birds can thresh, as רבה בר רב הונא asked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves birds can work from רבה בר רב הונא's question about threshing with geese and chickens.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, as רבה בר רב הונא asked: if someone threshed with geese and chickens, what is the law according to רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that birds can work, using a question asked by רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר רב הונא asked about threshing grain with geese and chickens, according to רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה. Whatever the answer is, the question itself assumes that birds can thresh. So birds can be used for work, and 'ורדו' can still mean work.
steps.whatToRemember: The pattern repeats: the גמרא shows that each creature in the פסוק (fish, birds) can be used for work, so 'ורדו' never has to mean eating.

phrases.aramaic: אִין, כִּדְבָעֵי רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Yes, as Rabba bar Rav Huna asked:
If one threshed with geese and chickens,
according to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The question is about the rule against muzzling an animal while it threshes. The point here is just that birds can thresh.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, כִּדְבָעֵי רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual proof that the challenge's assumption is wrong (birds can work).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Birds cannot work, so 'ורדו' must mean eating.
steps.terutzMaskana: Birds can thresh, so 'ורדו' can mean work.

steps.title: A challenge from 'every creeping creature'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges from the end of the פסוק: ruling over creeping creatures cannot mean work, so it must mean eating.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'And over every living creature that creeps on the earth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more proof from the same פסוק, about creatures that creep on the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Creeping creatures surely cannot be used for work. So ruling over them seems to mean eating them. That would show אדם הראשון was allowed to eat meat.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"And over every living creature that creeps upon the earth."
phrases.notes: בראשית 1:28. The challenge is not said out loud: creeping creatures can't work, so this must mean eating.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: וּבְכׇל חַיָּה הָרֹמֶשֶׂת עַל הָאָרֶץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After fish and birds were answered, a harder challenge comes from creeping creatures.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'ורדו' means work, and so רב's view.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Creeping creatures cannot work, so ruling over them must mean eating them.

steps.title: That phrase comes to include the snake
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this phrase comes to include the נחש, which could be used for work.
steps.simpleTranslation: That phrase comes to include the snake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'every creeping creature' is there to include the נחש. So it is still about work, not eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase does not mean all creeping creatures for eating. It comes to add the נחש, which, when it was created, could be used for work. So 'ורדו' still means work, and רב's view stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Every part of 'ורדו' (fish, birds, creeping creatures) is explained as being about work. So the פסוק does not prove that אדם הראשון was allowed to eat meat, and רב's view stands.

phrases.english: That phrase is to include the snake
is what it comes for.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the פסוק to a specific case (the נחש).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Every creeping creature' means eating creeping creatures.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase includes the נחש, which could work, so it is still about work.

steps.title: The snake could have been a great servant
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from רבי שמעון בן מנסיא shows that, before its curse, the נחש could have done real work for people.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי שמעון בן מנסיא says: What a loss, a great servant is gone from the world! If the snake had not been cursed, every Jew would have had two good snakes. He would send one north and one south to bring him fine jewels and pearls. On top of that, he could tie a strap under its tail and use it to carry dirt to his garden and his ruined building.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up the last answer, that the נחש could be used for work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 30 the גמרא said the phrase about ruling over creeping creatures includes the נחש, because it could work. This ברייתא shows that this is true. Before its curse, the נחש could fetch jewels and haul dirt like a work animal.

keyTerms.meaning: They tie a strap, like a harness

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן מְנַסְיָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says:
Woe over a great servant
that has been lost from the world,
for if the snake had not been cursed,
each and every one of Israel

phrases.aramaic: הָיוּ מִזְדַּמְּנִין לוֹ שְׁנֵי נְחָשִׁים טוֹבִים –
phrases.english: would have had two fine snakes ready for him.
One he would send to the north
and one he would send to the south,
to bring him fine sandalbonim
and precious stones and pearls.
And not only that, but
they would tie a strap under its tail
and with it, it would carry dirt out to his garden and to his ruin.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 30's claim that the נחש could be used for work.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that ruling over creeping creatures includes the נחש, which could do work.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן מנסיא describing the uncursed snake as a servant.
steps.whatToRemember: Before its curse, the נחש could have served people like a work animal. So 'ruling over' creatures can mean using them for work, not eating them.

steps.title: Angels roasted meat for אדם
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says angels roasted meat for אדם הראשון, which seems to show he was allowed to eat meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised a challenge: רבי יהודה בן תימא used to say: אדם הראשון would dine in גן עדן, and the angels would roast meat for him and strain wine for him. The snake looked at him, saw his honor, and became jealous of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that אדם הראשון was not allowed to eat meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the סוגיא said אדם was only allowed plants, and meat was first allowed in נח's time. But this ברייתא says the מלאכי השרת roasted meat for him. That sounds like he ate meat.

phrases.aramaic: מֵיתִיבִי, הָיָה רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן תֵּימָא אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: They raised a challenge: Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima would say:

phrases.aramaic: אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן מֵיסֵב בְּגַן עֵדֶן הָיָה,
phrases.english: Adam, the first man, would dine in the Garden of Eden,
and the ministering angels would

phrases.aramaic: צוֹלִין לוֹ בָּשָׂר וּמְסַנְּנִין לוֹ יַיִן.
phrases.english: roast meat for him and strain wine for him.
The snake peeked at him and saw his honor,
and became jealous of him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to challenge רב's statement from step 15, this time from a ברייתא instead of a פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier position that meat was forbidden to אדם הראשון.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If angels roasted meat for אדם, then he was eating meat.

steps.title: It was meat from heaven
steps.stepSummary: The meat the angels roasted was not from an animal. It came down from heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: There it is talking about meat that came down from heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. אדם's meat was a special meat from heaven, not meat from a slaughtered animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב learned from the פסוק that the animals of the earth are not food for אדם. Meat that came down from heaven does not come from any animal of the earth, so it does not go against רב's statement.

keyTerms.meaning: Meat that comes down from heaven

phrases.english: There it is talking about meat that comes down from heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the meat was not animal meat.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The angels roasted ordinary animal meat for אדם.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was heavenly meat, so אדם was still not eating animals.

steps.title: Is there really meat from heaven?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether meat that comes down from heaven really exists.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there such a thing as meat that comes down from heaven?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer just given, and sets up a story that will prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 33 depends on heavenly meat being real. The גמרא wants to see an example before it accepts the answer.

phrases.aramaic: מִי אִיכָּא בָּשָׂר הַיּוֹרֵד מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם?
phrases.english: Is there such a thing as meat that comes down from heaven?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אִיכָּא בָּשָׂר הַיּוֹרֵד מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether the answer of step 33 is realistic.

steps.title: רבי שמעון בן חלפתא and the lions
steps.stepSummary: A story shows that meat once came down from heaven, and the חכמים ruled it was kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. Here is a story: רבי שמעון בן חלפתא was walking on the road. Some lions met him and roared at him. He said: 'The young lions roar for prey.' Two thighs came down from heaven for him. The lions ate one and left the other. He took it to the בית מדרש and asked: Is this a non-kosher thing or a kosher thing? They told him: No non-kosher thing comes down from heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers yes and proves it with a story where meat came down from heaven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן חלפתא quoted the פסוק that lions get their food from ה׳, and meat came down for them. This shows heavenly meat is real. The חכמים also added a rule: anything that comes down from heaven is kosher.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'אין דבר טמא יורד מן השמים' is the base for the next question about a donkey-shaped piece of meat.

phrases.english: Yes, like this story:

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן חֲלַפְתָּא הֲוָה קָאָזֵיל בְּאוֹרְחָא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta was walking on the road,
and some lions came upon him
that were roaring at him.
He said: "The young lions roar for prey."
phrases.notes: תהלים 104:21. The פסוק goes on to say they ask ה׳ for their food.

phrases.english: Two thighs came down for him.
One they ate, and one they left.
He took it and came to the study hall,
and asked about it:

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר טָמֵא הוּא זֶה אוֹ דָּבָר טָהוֹר?
phrases.english: Is this a non-kosher thing or a kosher thing?
They said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין דָּבָר טָמֵא יוֹרֵד מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם.
phrases.english: No non-kosher thing comes down from heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, כִּי הָא דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן חֲלַפְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 34's question with a real case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, heavenly meat exists, as in the story of רבי שמעון בן חלפתא. Such meat is always kosher.
steps.whatToRemember: Meat can come down from heaven, and the חכמים said anything that comes down from heaven is kosher. This is how the גמרא explains the meat the angels gave אדם.

steps.title: What if it looked like a donkey?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks what the law would be if the heavenly meat had the form of a non-kosher animal, like a donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked רבי אבהו: If something shaped like a donkey had come down for him, what would the law be?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks a follow-up question about the story. The next step gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A donkey is a non-kosher animal. רבי זירא wants to know if heavenly meat that looks like a non-kosher animal would still be allowed.

phrases.aramaic: בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked Rabbi Abbahu:
If the form of a donkey came down for him, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא מֵרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the rule from the story in step 35.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether heavenly meat shaped like a non-kosher animal is allowed.

steps.title: רבי אבהו: the rule already answers this
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו calls the question foolish, because the חכמים already said nothing non-kosher comes down from heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Foolish bird! They already told him: No non-kosher thing comes down from heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers that the question was already settled by the rule of the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule has no exceptions: anything that comes down from heaven is kosher. So even a donkey shape would be allowed, and רבי אבהו sees the question as obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: Foolish bird, a sharp way of calling a question silly

phrases.english: He said to him: Foolish bird!
phrases.notes: This is a sharp nickname. רבי אבהו means the answer should have been obvious.

phrases.english: Surely they already told him:
phrases.notes: "Him" means רבי שמעון בן חלפתא, from the story in the בית מדרש.

phrases.aramaic: אֵין דָּבָר טָמֵא יוֹרֵד מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם.
phrases.english: No non-kosher thing comes down from heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's question in step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Even a donkey shape would be kosher, because nothing non-kosher comes down from heaven.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule is complete: whatever comes down from heaven is kosher, no matter what shape it has.

steps.title: רבי שמעון adds sorcery to the Noahide מצוות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי שמעון from the ברייתא: בני נח are also commanded not to practice כישוף.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: they were also commanded about sorcery.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting רבי שמעון's opinion from the ברייתא about the מצוות of בני נח. He adds one more prohibition: כישוף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists the basic מצוות that every non-Jew must keep. רבי שמעון holds that the list is longer and also includes a ban on כישוף. Now that his opinion is on the table, the גמרא can ask where it comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: Descendants of נח, meaning all non-Jews

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
Also concerning sorcery.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: אַף עַל הַכִּישּׁוּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of heavenly meat and starts a new section on another Noahide מצוה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון, בני נח are forbidden to practice כישוף.

steps.title: What is רבי שמעון's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind רבי שמעון's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי שמעון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי שמעון learns that בני נח are forbidden to do כישוף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prohibition of כישוף appears in the תורה as a command to the Jewish people. So the גמרא needs a source showing that it also applies to non-Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: What is his reason? A request for the source

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the ruling just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק teaches that בני נח are commanded not to do כישוף.

steps.title: The answer begins with a verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to answer by introducing a פסוק. The פסוק itself comes in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its answer: it is about to quote a פסוק as רבי שמעון's source. The פסוק follows right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "it is written" tells us the source will be a פסוק, not logic. We have to see the next words to learn how the פסוק shows that כישוף is forbidden to בני נח.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written, introducing a פסוק

phrases.english: As it is written:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts to answer the question about רבי שמעון's source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is a פסוק, which is quoted in the continuation.
